Chapter 2: The Weight of Language and the Struggle to Belong
Language—it’s so much more than just words, isn’t it? It’s how we connect with each other, how we show the world who we are, and how we carve out a place for ourselves. But what happens when the language you grew up with isn’t the one that’s valued by those in power?
Imagine a young person, eager to prove themselves, sitting in a classroom where the teacher demands perfect grammar and a flawless accent. Every time they search for the right words, they feel all eyes on them. There’s that sting of embarrassment, like being put under a spotlight. The message is loud and clear—you want respect? Then you’ve got to sound like the people in charge.
But at home, it’s a whole different story. The language there is filled with warmth, laughter, and memories. It’s the language of comfort. Yet, step outside, and suddenly that same language is something to hide. This young person starts correcting their parents, maybe even tries to lose their accent, or avoids speaking their own language in public altogether. It’s not about rejecting their roots—it’s just a desperate attempt to fit in.
And here’s the thing—it’s not really about words at all. It’s about power. The language of the colonizer, or the dominant group, becomes your ticket to opportunity. If you want to be seen as worthy, you have to use the “right” words. But every time you do, you leave a little piece of yourself behind. The more you succeed, the greater the gap feels between who you are, and who you’re expected to be.
So many people end up living in two worlds. They become experts at code-switching, slipping between languages—and even identities—depending on where they are. In some circles, they’re celebrated for their eloquence, for supposedly “rising above” their background. In others, they’re accused of forgetting where they came from.
The pressure never really lets up. It’s not just about speaking the language, it’s about speaking it perfectly, without a single trace of difference. Any little slip, any hint of an accent, feels like a mark against you. And that fear—of being found out, of being seen as less—lingers, no matter how hard you try.
Over time, this struggle with language becomes a struggle with yourself. The hunger to belong, to be accepted, can lead you to erase parts of who you are. You start to wonder—will I ever be enough? Will I ever really belong anywhere? The world rewards people who hide their differences, but at what cost?
Still, even in the middle of all this, there are moments of quiet resistance. Maybe it’s a joke shared in the old language, a song sung at a family gathering, or just refusing to apologize for who you are. These small acts? They become lifelines—a way to hold onto dignity, to claim your space in a world that would rather you blend in.
So, it’s crystal clear—language is never just neutral. It carries the weight of history, of power, and of belonging. The real challenge isn’t just mastering the words. It’s finding a way to speak that lets you be seen—without disappearing.
